content: The guidelines will be made accessible on the WHO website, specifically on the WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety page. These guidelines will also be distributed during meetings and scientific conferences attended by WHO staff. Social media platforms will be utilized to raise awareness about the updated recommendations. UNICEF and WHO are leading a Global Breastfeeding Collective to enhance political commitment to breastfeeding, which is considered one of the most effective investments a country can make. This initiative focuses on promoting early initiation of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, and continued breastfeeding for up to two years or beyond, alongside the provision of appropriate, adequate, and safe complementary foods. This effort will also help disseminate the recommendations outlined in the guidelines. The executive summary of the guidelines may be translated into the other five official United Nations languages and distributed through WHO regional offices. Technical assistance will be provided to any WHO regional office interested in translating the full guidelines into these languages and supporting countries in implementing them effectively. All stakeholders involved in infant care in regions with Zika virus transmission, at international, national, and local levels, should consider disseminating and implementing the recommendations provided in these guidelines. Improving the implementation of these recommendations requires the development of policies and stronger regulatory frameworks to support breastfeeding. The Guideline Development Group has identified significant knowledge gaps that need to be addressed through primary research, as these gaps may influence the recommendations. Further research is required to explore the resources, feasibility, acceptability, and equity of modifying infant feeding practices for infants affected by complications associated with the Zika virus. Additionally, research is needed to determine the type of additional support required for caregivers of these infants, as no direct evidence currently exists. Key research questions include: Determining the viral load necessary for Zika virus transmission through breast milk. Understanding the perspectives of pregnant women, mothers, family members, healthcare practitioners, policymakers, and midwives regarding infant feeding when there is a risk of Zika virus transmission. Assessing how breastfeeding or feeding breast milk from a lactating woman infected with the Zika virus impacts health equity. Evaluating the acceptability and feasibility of breastfeeding or feeding breast milk to infants from a lactating woman infected with the Zika virus. Investigating how modifications in infant feeding affect critical infant outcomes among those affected by Zika virus-related complications, and evaluating the resources, feasibility, acceptability, and equity of these modifications. Examining how additional support and follow-up for caregivers influence improvements in infant feeding among those affected by Zika virus-related complications, and evaluating the resources, feasibility, acceptability, continuity, and equity of this support. Implementing recommendations to breastfeed or provide breast milk to all infants born to mothers with suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection, or who reside in or have traveled to areas with ongoing Zika virus transmission, requires staff training and time to provide counseling as part of routine antenatal and postnatal care services. Interventions for modifying infant feeding and providing additional support for caregivers of infants affected by Zika virus-related complications require resources for staff training, counseling, specialized foods, thickeners, therapeutic instruments, adaptive equipment (e.g., one-way slit-valve nipples, nosey cups, Maroon Spoons), and nasogastric or orogastric tube feeding. The implementation of these guidelines should be monitored at the health-service level as part of broader efforts to improve the quality of healthcare for children. Continuous screening of mothers and infants in areas of Zika virus transmission is essential to identify potential harm or adverse events. Data disaggregated by socioeconomic variables should be included to understand which groups are more affected or vulnerable to the outbreak and may require additional support for breastfeeding or infant feeding. WHO will continue to monitor research developments in infant feeding in areas of Zika virus transmission, particularly regarding the availability of a Zika virus vaccine. WHO will maintain a dynamic system to prioritize normative global goods for country impact and will conduct literature surveillance to respond rapidly to changes in Zika virus epidemiology and emerging evidence. This ensures that accurate, relevant, and up-to-date guidance is available to Member States and their global partners.
